papers.headline: Silencing a liver enzyme protects mice from a toxic metabolic disease
papers.original_title: Rescue of glutaric aciduria type I by GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase
papers.reason: Liver-targeted siRNA silencing an upstream lysine-degradation enzyme rescues a mouse model of glutaric aciduria type I.
papers.summary:
Glutaric aciduria type I (GA-1) is an inherited disease in which a missing enzyme, glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, blocks one step in the breakdown of the amino acid lysine. Toxic organic acids build up and damage a brain region called the striatum, causing movement problems. Even with newborn screening and special diets, about a third of patients still develop serious neurological damage. The researchers' idea was to cut off the problem at its source: block an earlier enzyme in the lysine breakdown pathway, aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase (AASS), so the toxic acids are never made.

They used a small interfering RNA (siRNA) — a short RNA that shuts down production of a specific protein — linked to a sugar tag (GalNAc) that steers it into liver cells. Giving this to newborn mice lacking the GCDH enzyme prevented deaths, reduced brain damage, and lowered toxic metabolites in the brain and other tissues. Blood levels of glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and glutarylcarnitine tracked how well the mice did neurologically, suggesting they could be used to monitor treatment. Oddly, the metabolites stayed high in urine even as blood levels fell, which the authors attribute to the kidneys continuing to flush out stored metabolite.
papers.why_it_matters: GalNAc-linked siRNAs are already an established way to switch off liver genes in humans, so this approach could plausibly be translated to patients with GA-1. It also illustrates a general strategy for metabolic diseases: instead of replacing a broken enzyme, slow down the pathway feeding into it. The blood markers identified here could let doctors check whether such a treatment is working.
papers.limitations: This was done in genetically modified mice, not people, and treatment began in newborns, so it is unclear whether it would help patients already showing symptoms. The abstract does not report long-term safety or effects of lowering lysine breakdown over time.

papers.headline: Gentle brain stimulation at alpha rhythm boosts reward learning and eases low mood
papers.original_title: Temporal interference stimulation targeting the ventromedial prefrontal cortex enhances reward learning and improves depression scores
papers.reason: Noninvasive temporal interference stimulation of deep reward circuitry enhanced reward learning and improved depression scores.
papers.summary:
Learning from rewards relies on brain circuits linking the front of the brain to deeper structures. A key signal is the reward prediction error: the gap between the reward you expected and the reward you actually got. Problems in these circuits are linked to conditions such as depression, but deep brain areas are hard to reach without surgery. The researchers used brain scans and computer models in healthy adults to study how the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (a region just behind the forehead) and the ventral striatum (a deeper reward hub) interact during learning. They then tested a non-invasive method called temporal interference stimulation, which uses electrical currents applied through the scalp to target deeper brain tissue.

The two regions formed a two-way loop, one side exciting and the other inhibiting, that tracked prediction errors. The strength of this loop matched how quickly each person learned. Brain rhythms in the alpha and theta ranges in the prefrontal region also followed reward errors, but no matching pattern was found for learning from punishment. Stimulating the prefrontal region at an alpha rhythm (10 hertz) improved reward learning and changed how the two regions connected, while a theta rhythm (5 hertz) did nothing. In a randomized trial of 69 people with mild, below-diagnosis-level depression, three daily alpha sessions reduced depressive symptoms, and some of the benefit only appeared at a 7-day follow-up.
papers.why_it_matters: Reaching deep reward circuits usually requires surgery or drugs, so a scalp-based method that seems to influence them could open new treatment options. Because it targets a specific circuit and rhythm, it may also help explain how reward learning goes wrong in depression.
papers.limitations: The clinical trial involved 69 people with mild, below-diagnosis-level symptoms and only three days of stimulation, so it is unclear whether the effects would hold for clinical depression or last over the longer term.

key_terms.meaning: The difference between an expected reward and the one actually received; the brain uses it to update what it learns.

papers.headline: Atlantic Gulf Stream changes can warm the North Pacific through the Arctic air
papers.original_title: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
papers.reason: Model simulations show Gulf Stream variability influences Kuroshio Extension warming via an Arctic atmospheric bridge, contributing to recent North Pacific warming.
papers.summary:
In recent years, ocean surface temperatures have run unusually high across much of the Northern Hemisphere outside the tropics. Scientists usually look to the tropical Pacific to explain swings in the North Pacific, but whether the North Atlantic at mid-latitudes also plays a part has been unclear. This study asked whether changes in the Gulf Stream (the strong warm current off the US East Coast) can affect the Kuroshio Extension (a similar warm current flowing east from Japan). The team used simplified, idealized climate model runs spanning 100 years.

In the simulations, Gulf Stream changes accounted for about 13% of the natural, internally generated year-to-year variation in Kuroshio Extension surface temperature. The influence ran one way only: the model gave no sign that the Kuroshio affected the Gulf Stream. When the Gulf Stream region was warmer than usual, the atmosphere responded with a pattern resembling the Northern Annular Mode, a hemisphere-wide see-saw in air pressure centred on the Arctic. This pattern weakened the Aleutian Low, a persistent low-pressure system over the North Pacific. The Kuroshio Extension then moved northward and carried more warm water north, warming the western North Pacific. The link only appeared properly when the ocean model had high resolution, fine enough to capture sharp ocean fronts.
papers.why_it_matters: The work points to a route by which the Atlantic can influence Pacific temperatures through the atmosphere, and the authors suggest it helped drive the exceptional North Pacific warmth of 2020–2024. Because ocean currents change slowly, this link might help forecasters predict Northern Hemisphere climate years to decades ahead.
papers.limitations: The results come from idealized model simulations, and the Gulf Stream explains only a modest share (13%) of Kuroshio Extension variation. The link also depends on using a high-resolution ocean model, so coarser climate models may miss it.

papers.headline: Pairing home energy upgrades with solar could help poorer households save more
papers.original_title: Targeted technology coadoption for reconciling energy savings and equity gains in the residential energy transition
papers.reason: Shows that targeted solar co-adoption for disadvantaged households can reconcile energy savings with equity gains in the residential energy transition.
papers.summary:
Moving homes away from fossil fuels relies on technologies such as rooftop solar panels and efficient appliances, but these tend to end up in wealthier homes. This study asks whether choosing who gets these technologies, and which ones they get together, can cut overall energy use while also easing energy costs for disadvantaged households.

The short publisher description reports that when technology rollout is aimed at lowering energy burden (the share of a household's income spent on energy), the technologies shift toward disadvantaged households. It also reports that having these households adopt solar alongside other technologies can make energy costs fairer. The authors conclude that policies should bundle technologies together and be designed so that people in apartment buildings and renters can take part.
papers.why_it_matters: If clean-energy upgrades mostly reach better-off homeowners, the energy transition could widen gaps in what households pay for energy. This work suggests that careful targeting and bundling of technologies could advance both energy savings and fairness.
papers.limitations: Only a brief summary is available, so the study's methods, data, location and the size of the reported effects are unclear.

key_terms.meaning: The portion of a household's income that goes to paying for energy such as electricity and heating.
A household installing two or more energy technologies together, for example solar panels alongside another upgrade.
Improvements in fairness, here meaning that benefits reach households that are struggling most with energy costs.
Buildings with several separate homes, such as apartment blocks, where individual residents often cannot install rooftop solar on their own.

papers.headline: Damaged lysosomes form internal protein clumps that slow leakage of their contents
papers.original_title: Endolysosomal damage promotes intraluminal protein condensate formation that limits cytosolic leakage
papers.reason: Damaged endolysosomes rapidly form intraluminal protein condensates that limit cytosolic leakage, a finding relevant to antisense oligonucleotide delivery.
papers.summary:
Endolysosomes are small membrane-bound compartments inside cells that break down material taken in from outside. When their membranes get damaged, their contents can spill into the cytosol, the fluid that fills the cell, and this can harm the cell. Until now, scientists did not know what actually happens to those contents during damage, or how much of them really leaks out. This study, done in mammalian cells, looked inside damaged endolysosomes.

The researchers found that membrane damage quickly causes some of the proteins normally living inside these compartments to gather into dense clumps called condensates. Electron microscopy showed a distinctive look inside the damaged compartments. Cryo-electron tomography, a 3D imaging method for frozen, near-natural samples, confirmed that the clumps are tightly packed. The clumps formed under several different kinds of membrane damage, and they broke apart again when the compartments recovered. The condensates also trapped therapeutic oligonucleotides (short synthetic DNA or RNA drugs) and held them in place, so these drugs stayed stuck inside even though the membrane was damaged.
papers.why_it_matters: Oligonucleotide drugs must escape from endolysosomes into the cytosol to work, and poor escape is a major hurdle for them. Knowing that protein condensates physically hold these drugs back suggests a new target for making such therapies more effective. It also shows that cells may have a built-in way to limit harmful leakage when these compartments break.
papers.limitations: The abstract describes cell-level experiments. It does not show whether blocking condensate formation actually improves drug performance in animals or patients. Only part of the resident proteins form condensates, and the abstract does not explain what controls which ones do.

key_terms.meaning: A membrane-bound compartment inside cells that receives material from outside the cell and breaks it down.
A dense, membrane-free cluster of proteins (and sometimes other molecules) that forms when they come together out of a surrounding solution.
The fluid part of the cell's interior, outside the organelles.
An imaging technique that builds 3D pictures of rapidly frozen samples, keeping structures close to their natural state.
Drugs made of short stretches of DNA or RNA that act on genes or their messages inside cells.

papers.headline: An aging-related plant protein helps a heat-response protein survive in warm weather
papers.original_title: ORE1 stabilizes PIF4 protein through a UBP12/UBP13-dependent regulatory module in thermomorphogenesis
papers.reason: Published today, the study shows a senescence factor stabilizes the heat regulator PIF4 to drive warmth-induced plant growth.
papers.summary:
Plants change how they grow when temperatures rise, for example by stretching their stems, a response called thermomorphogenesis. A key controller of this response is a protein called PIF4. The researchers asked how signals tied to plant aging (senescence) might affect how long PIF4 lasts inside cells, a question that had not been settled.

They report that ORE1, a protein previously known for its role in senescence, works as a scaffold, a kind of molecular platform that brings other proteins together. ORE1 links PIF4 with two enzymes, UBP12 and UBP13, which remove ubiquitin tags from proteins. Because ubiquitin tags normally mark proteins for destruction, removing them keeps PIF4 stable. More PIF4 then drives the extra growth plants show in warmth.
papers.why_it_matters: The work connects two processes usually studied separately, plant aging and the response to heat, through control of protein stability. Knowing how plants manage their growth in warm conditions could help in understanding and eventually improving crop performance as temperatures rise.
papers.limitations: The publisher's summary does not name the plant species or describe the experiments, so it is unclear how widely the findings apply, for example to crops or field conditions.

key_terms.meaning: Changes in plant shape and growth, such as longer stems, triggered by warmer temperatures.
A plant protein that switches on genes driving growth responses to heat.
The aging process in plant tissues, such as leaf yellowing and breakdown.
Attaching or removing small ubiquitin tags on proteins; the tags often mark a protein to be destroyed.
A protein that holds other proteins together so they can interact.

papers.headline: Brain scans with millisecond timing show how we come to feel a limb is ours
papers.original_title: Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception
papers.reason: Published today, magnetoencephalography maps how cortical and cerebellar networks are engaged in sequence when a hand feels like one's own.
papers.summary:
How does the brain produce the feeling that our arm belongs to us? Earlier work mostly used fMRI (which tracks blood flow and is slow) or studied patients with brain damage, giving a fairly frozen snapshot of the regions involved. This study used magnetoencephalography (MEG), which picks up the brain's tiny magnetic signals with very fine timing. While participants were in the scanner, a robot delivered matched touches that they could see and feel. Testing included the rubber hand illusion, in which a fake hand starts to feel like one's own, plus a condition with the person's real hand and several control conditions. A pattern-based analysis then looked for brain activity that tracked feeling ownership of the left arm.

Ownership-related activity unfolded in three stages. Before the touch even happened, there were anticipatory patterns in the middle of the frontal lobe, the right rear parietal lobe and the right rear cerebellum. About 116–156 milliseconds after the touch, regions thought to combine vision and touch became involved: right premotor areas (which help plan movement), the right posterior parietal cortex and the front of the cerebellum. Later, around 184–232 milliseconds, patterns appeared in the insula on both sides and in areas of the left hemisphere.
papers.why_it_matters: The work gives a whole-brain, time-resolved picture of body ownership, showing it is assembled step by step rather than switched on in one place. This could help explain disorders where people feel a limb is not theirs, and may inform the design of prosthetics or virtual bodies that feel like part of the self.
papers.limitations: The abstract does not give the number of participants, and the findings concern ownership of the left arm only. MEG pinpoints locations less precisely than fMRI, so the identified regions are estimates.

key_terms.meaning: The sense that a body part belongs to you.
An experiment where a hidden real hand and a visible fake hand are touched at the same time, so the fake hand begins to feel like one's own.
A method that measures the magnetic fields produced by brain activity, capturing changes over milliseconds.
Statistics that examine patterns across many measurements at once, instead of one signal at a time.
Touch that a person both sees and feels, used here to create the illusion.
The brain combining information from different senses, such as sight and touch, into one experience.

papers.headline: How Baltic Sea plankton and weather shape gases swapped with the air
papers.original_title: Marine volatile organic compounds air-sea exchange dynamics across a summer-to-autumn ecosystem transition
papers.reason: Published today, continuous measurements in the Baltic Sea show how phytoplankton and physical processes shape volatile organic compound air–sea exchange as summer turns to autumn.
papers.summary:
Seawater both gives off and absorbs many small carbon-containing gases called volatile organic compounds (VOCs). This study asked how this two-way exchange between ocean and air changes as the seasons shift from summer to autumn, when the community of microscopic algae (phytoplankton) in the water also changes.

The researchers ran continuous measurements of VOC exchange at an island in the Baltic Sea across this seasonal transition. According to the publisher's summary, they found that the release and uptake of a wide range of VOCs were controlled jointly by phytoplankton activity and by physical processes in the water and air, rather than by either factor alone. The short description available does not give specific compounds, amounts or rates.
papers.why_it_matters: VOCs released from the sea can react in the atmosphere and help form tiny particles that affect clouds and climate, so knowing what drives their exchange helps improve climate and air-quality models. Showing how both living organisms and physical conditions matter, and how this shifts with the seasons, gives a more realistic picture of the ocean's role in the atmosphere.
papers.limitations: Only a brief summary is available, so details of the methods and findings are unclear; the measurements come from a single Baltic Sea island site over one seasonal transition, which may not represent other seas or years.

key_terms.meaning: Carbon-based chemicals that evaporate easily and can move between water and air as gases.
The movement of gases from the ocean into the atmosphere (emission) or from the atmosphere into the ocean (uptake).
Microscopic algae and other photosynthesising organisms drifting in surface water.
A seasonal shift in the conditions and living communities of an environment, here from summer to autumn.

papers.headline: Words people use often are more likely to exist across many languages
papers.original_title: Usage frequency predicts lexicalization across languages
papers.reason: Finds that how often a concept is used in communication predicts whether languages have a dedicated word for it.
papers.summary:
Some ideas, like CHILD or SUN, have their own dedicated word in nearly every language, while others, like PARENT or WEATHER, often do not. The researchers asked why: in particular, whether concepts that people talk about more often are more likely to get their own word, a process linguists call lexicalization.

They studied 854 concepts. They measured how often each concept is used, on average, in recorded speech and text from 46 languages in a documentation corpus. They then compared this with how many languages have a dedicated word for the concept, using two separate word collections: one covering 41 languages and one covering 262 languages. In both comparisons, concepts that are used more often were more likely to have their own word. The statistical link was moderate (standardized effects of about 0.25 and 0.30), with confidence ranges well above zero.
papers.why_it_matters: The results suggest that the similarities in vocabulary across the world's languages come partly from people in different cultures talking about similar things with similar frequency. This links everyday language use to the long-term shape of what languages choose to name.
papers.limitations: This is a correlational analysis, so it shows that frequency predicts whether a word exists but does not prove that frequency causes it. Frequency explained only part of the pattern, and the frequency data came from a sample of 46 languages.

key_terms.meaning: When a language has a dedicated word or fixed expression for a concept, rather than describing it with a phrase.
How often a concept comes up when people actually speak or write.
How common a feature, here having a word for a concept, is across the world's languages.
A number giving the strength of the relationship between a predictor and an outcome in a statistical model. Larger values mean a stronger link.
A range of values that likely contains the true effect size, given the data.

papers.headline: Complete pig genomes reveal moving centromeres and genes behind high-altitude adaptation
papers.original_title: High-quality pig pan-genome resources illuminate centromere evolution and enhance genotype–phenotype mapping
papers.reason: Telomere-to-telomere pig genomes, integrated with transcriptomic and metabolomic data, illuminate centromere evolution and improve genotype–phenotype mapping for breeding.
papers.summary:
Most pig genetics relies on a single reference genome that still has gaps, especially in hard-to-read repetitive regions such as centromeres (the chromosome 'waist' that guides chromosome separation during cell division). The researchers assembled genomes from 19 pig breeds chosen from different climates, including cold-tolerant, heat- and humidity-tolerant and Tibetan high-altitude pigs. Three of these are telomere-to-telomere (T2T), meaning every chromosome is read end to end with no gaps. They paired the genomes with RNA and metabolite measurements from nine tissues, protein-binding maps that locate centromeres, and 3D chromosome-contact data.

In 12 boars, the Y-chromosome centromere sat in an unusual non-repetitive stretch of DNA. Its exact position split the breeds into two groups that matched their family tree and roughly fell south and north of the Yangtze River. Centromere position tracked how far a nearby repeated DNA block had expanded. Chromosome 1 centromeres shifted often, and a highly active gene, eEF1A1, sits near chromosome breakage and fusion points in several mammals. Combining 31 pig genomes gave about 230,000 large DNA changes (structural variants). One of them, a 300-base insertion in front of the AKR1B1 gene in Tibetan pigs, reduced gene activity in a reporter test. Lowering AKR1B1 in pig kidney cells grown at low oxygen increased cell growth and reduced cell death. A graph-style pan-genome built on a T2T reference explained slightly more of the inherited variation in about 2,000 molecular traits measured in 334 Yorkshire pigs.
papers.why_it_matters: These gap-free genomes give pig breeders and biomedical researchers a more accurate reference, including regions that were previously unreadable. The Y-chromosome centromere is passed only from father to son, so its position could serve as a stable marker of pig ancestry. Including large DNA changes, not just single-letter differences, may help link genes to traits for breeding.
papers.limitations: The AKR1B1 role in altitude adaptation rests on cell-culture and reporter experiments, not tests in living pigs. The authors note that sorting out how environment, domestication and Y-chromosome decay each drive centromere movement will require more breeds. The eEF1A1 link to chromosome breakage is a correlation-based hypothesis.

key_terms.meaning: A combined genome collection from many individuals or breeds, capturing variation that a single reference genome misses.
A genome assembly in which each chromosome is fully read from one end to the other with no gaps.
A shift in where the centromere sits along a chromosome during evolution.
A large DNA change, such as an insertion, deletion or flipped segment, typically 50 bases or longer.
The share of variation in a trait across individuals that can be explained by genetic differences.
A low-oxygen condition, such as at high altitude.
